usage: Points to something near the speaker. Written/formal form of 이거.
이것 + 이. In speech this often becomes 이게.
이것 + 을. In speech this often becomes 이걸.
이것 + 은. In speech this often becomes 이건.
examples: 이것 marks something close to the speaker.
Formal way to ask about a nearby object.
Pointing at something right in front of you.
nuance: 이것 means 'this thing' and refers to an object close to the speaker. It is the fuller, slightly more formal form, while 이거 is the everyday spoken version. In writing or polite situations you will see 이것, but in casual talk Koreans usually say 이거.
mistakes: Using 이것 for a person — for people use a name or 이분/이 사람, not 이것.
Forgetting that 이것이/이것을/이것은 contract to 이게/이걸/이건 in everyday speech.

usage: Points to something near the listener, or something already mentioned.
그것 + 이. Often becomes 그게 in speech.
그것 + 을. Often becomes 그걸 in speech.
그것 + 은. Often becomes 그건 in speech.
examples: Asking about something near the listener.
그것 can point to a thing the listener has.
Asking for an item close to the other person.
nuance: 그것 means 'that thing' and points to something near the listener, or to something both people already talked about. The spoken form is 그거. Korean splits 'that' into 그것 (near you / already mentioned) and 저것 (far from both of us), so picking the right one depends on distance.
mistakes: Using 그것 for something far from both speakers — that situation needs 저것.
Saying 그것이 in casual conversation where 그게 sounds far more natural.

usage: Points to something far from both speaker and listener.
저것 + 이. Often becomes 저게 in speech.
저것 + 을. Often becomes 저걸 in speech.
저것 + 은. Often becomes 저건 in speech.
examples: Both people are looking at something far away.
That one over there is prettier.
Please look at that over there.
nuance: 저것 means 'that thing over there' and points to something far from both the speaker and the listener. The casual spoken form is 저거. Remember the three-way set: 이것 (here), 그것 (near you), 저것 (over there) — Korean is more precise about distance than English 'this/that'.
mistakes: Using 저것 for something the listener is holding — that is 그것, not 저것.
Confusing 저것 (object) with 저기 (place over there).

usage: Everyday spoken form of 이것. Use this in normal conversation.
Contraction of 이거 + 가. Very common in speech.
examples: Pointing at an item when shopping or ordering.
The most natural way to ask a price.
nuance: 이거 is the casual, everyday version of 이것 and means 'this thing' near the speaker. This is the form you will actually hear and use most in daily life — shopping, ordering food, pointing at things. It contracts to 이게 (subject), 이걸 (object), and 이건 (topic) in fast speech.
mistakes: Writing 이거 in formal documents — formal writing prefers 이것.
Saying 이거가 instead of the natural contraction 이게.

examples: Asking for something near the listener.
Casual question about a thing close to you.
nuance: 그거 is the casual form of 그것 and points to something near the listener or already mentioned. It is extremely common in conversation and contracts to 그게, 그걸, 그건. Koreans also use 그거 to mean 'that thing we talked about' when both people already know what it is.
mistakes: Using 그거 for a distant object that the listener is not near — use 저거 there.
Saying 그거를 in casual speech where 그걸 sounds more natural.

examples: Both people look at a far object.
I'll take that one over there.
Pointing at something on a far shelf.
That one over there is bigger.
nuance: 저거 is the casual form of 저것 and points to something far from both speaker and listener. Together with 이거 and 그거 it completes the everyday 'this/that' set. When you point across a room or a store at something distant, 저거 is the word you reach for.
mistakes: Mixing up 저거 (a thing over there) and 저기 (a place over there).
Using 저거 for an item the listener is holding — that should be 그거.

usage: A place far from both speaker and listener.
저기 + 에 for location or destination.
Used to politely get a stranger's or a server's attention.
Telling someone where something is located.
nuance: 저기 means 'over there,' a place far from both people, completing the set 여기 (here) / 거기 (there, near you) / 저기 (over there). It doubles as a soft attention-getter: 저기요 is how Koreans politely say 'excuse me' to a stranger or call a waiter. The filler 저기... also works like English 'um' when you hesitate.
mistakes: Using 저기 for a place near the listener — that is 거기.
Forgetting that 저기요 (excuse me) is more polite than just shouting 여기요 in some settings.

usage: Question word for things. The fuller form of 뭐.
무엇 + 이. Often spoken as 뭐가.
무엇 + 을. Often spoken as 뭘 or 뭐.
Polite question; in speech usually 뭐예요?
nuance: 무엇 means 'what' and is the full form used in writing and polite or formal speech. In everyday conversation Koreans almost always shorten it to 뭐 (and 뭘, 뭐가). Learning both matters: textbooks and signs use 무엇, but real talk uses 뭐.
mistakes: Using 무엇 in very casual chat where 뭐 sounds far more natural.
Saying 무엇을 좋아해요 fine, but dropping the marker as 뭐 좋아해요 in speech — both occur, just keep them consistent.

usage: Comes before a noun: 어느 + noun. Picks one out of several.
어느 + 것. The spoken form is 어느 거.
A very common 어느 + noun phrase.
Asking about direction or choice between two.
nuance: 어느 means 'which' and always sits in front of a noun, helping you choose one option out of several (어느 나라, 어느 것, 어느 쪽). It is different from 무슨, which asks 'what kind of' rather than picking from a known set. Use 어느 when the choices are limited and visible.
mistakes: Using 어느 alone like a pronoun — it needs a following noun (say 어느 것, not just 어느).
Confusing 어느 (which, from a set) with 무슨 (what kind of).

usage: Refers back to the subject of the sentence.
자기 (+의) 집. The 의 is usually dropped, so people just say 자기 집.
자기 + 가 in a subordinate clause.
Affectionate way couples address each other.
examples: 자기 refers back to the doer.
nuance: 자기 has two common everyday uses: it is a reflexive pronoun meaning 'oneself' (자기 일 = one's own work), and it is also a sweet way couples call each other, like 'honey' (자기야). Context makes the meaning clear. As a reflexive, it points back to the subject already mentioned in the sentence.
mistakes: Using 자기야 with strangers or coworkers — it is intimate and only for close partners.
Translating reflexive 자기 as 'myself' when it actually refers to the sentence's subject (often 'himself/herself').

usage: Someone who is not you or your group.
남 + 의 = belonging to another person.
nuance: 남 means 'another person' or 'others' — people outside your own group or family. It often carries the nuance of 'a stranger' or 'someone unrelated to me,' as in 남의 물건 (someone else's belongings). It contrasts with 자기 (oneself) and 우리 (we/us), drawing a line between insiders and outsiders.
mistakes: Confusing 남 (another person) with 남자 (a man) — they look similar but mean different things.
Using 남 for your own family or close friends; 남 implies someone outside your circle.

usage: First-person plural. Also used for 'my' in close relationships.
Koreans say 우리 집 even for their own family home.
nuance: 우리 means 'we / us / our,' but Koreans use it far more often than English 'our.' They say 우리 집 (our house), 우리 엄마 (our mom), even 우리 나라 (our country), where English would say 'my.' This reflects a culture that frames family and group as shared. The humble form 저희 is used in polite speech.
mistakes: Translating 우리 엄마 as 'our mom' when it usually just means 'my mom.'
Using 우리 in very polite situations where the humble 저희 is expected.

usage: Direction or side near the speaker.
이쪽 + 으로 to show direction of movement.
examples: 이쪽으로 shows the direction to move.
이쪽에 marks a location near the speaker.
nuance: 이쪽 means 'this way' or 'this side,' the direction near the speaker. It belongs to the set 이쪽 / 그쪽 / 저쪽 (this way / that way near you / that way over there), matching the 이/그/저 pattern. It is very handy for giving directions and guiding people, especially with 이쪽으로 오세요.
mistakes: Mixing up 이쪽 (direction/side) with 이것 (a thing) — 쪽 is about which way.
Using 이쪽 for a far direction; for 'over there' use 저쪽.
